2041.tone: Pre-tonological 1891 description of a Bantu C30 (Ngiri) language that is certainly tonal. Cambier defines the accent as 'l'élévation de la voix' plus lengthening, and distinguishes among accented syllables a 'syllabe grave' (marked by a grave accent, mounsè) and a 'syllabe aiguë' (acute surmounted by a grave, nsé̀té). One reading is classical prosodic usage, i.e. low- vs high-pitched accented syllables registered independently of the penultimate prominence. But the same acute and grave marks also appear on syllables that do not carry the accent on the same pages (éteï p. 2; mbékèlé, mankéma p. 3), and in French 'accent aigu'/'accent grave' on e are the ordinary vowel-quality diacritics, so 'syllabe aiguë/grave' may instead or also mean a close-é vs open-è syllable in a seven-vowel system (Motingea 1990: 141 gives 7 vowels for neighbouring Mbonji). The source is undecidable on this point; either way it gives no tone rules and no tone-based placement claim, and its penult placement statement is what is coded. Length does not attract the accent: unaccented long syllables are marked separately (djīou 'œil'), so the rule is quantity-insensitive as stated. The Mbonji sketch in Motingea 1990: 143 says only 'La tonologie est de type lingala'; Motingea 1990: 69 reports non-phonemic penultimate lengthening for neighbouring Libobi.

tn.translation: ACCENT. A peculiarity of the Iboko language is that the accent, besides the raising of the voice, most often involves a prolongation, a slowness of pronunciation, which makes the accented syllable a very long syllable. ... The accent ordinarily falls on the penultimate. ... A grave syllable that has the accent will be indicated by a grave accent. Ex. mounse 'white ant'. Finally an acute syllable that has the accent will be marked by an acute accent surmounted by a grave accent. Ex. nsete 'nail'.

2043.tone: Tonal language (H vs L plus rising/falling contours), handled by Mamet in a separate 'Tonologie' section headed 'ACCENT DE HAUTEUR': 'Le ton haut est indiqué par un accent aigu. Une voyelle non accentuée a le ton bas. Les tons variables sont indiqués de deux façons: pour les tons montants nous auront aá ou à, eé ou ě, etc.'. The intensity accent is explicitly kept apart from tone and called weak: 'L'accent d'intensité est, au reste, assez peu prononcé. Il importe de ne pas l'exagérer ni de le transformer en accent de hauteur.' Because a stress rule IS stated, the record is coded set by morphology (root-anchored stress) rather than tone or pitch accent; a reviewer who wants the tonal system to dominate the coding has the alternative here.

tn.translation: Tonology. PITCH ACCENT. High tone is marked with an acute accent. An unaccented vowel has low tone. The variable tones are marked in two ways: for rising tones we shall have aá or ǎ, eé or ě, etc.; for falling tones áa or â, ée or ê, etc. As far as possible we avoid having to represent triple tones, by doubling the vowels ... these triple-tone vowels come from contractions and are always long. ... The intensity accent is, moreover, rather weak. It is important not to exaggerate it nor to turn it into a pitch accent.

The occurrence of stress in any word is unpredictable but it defines a syllable on which it falls as being one of the three last syllables of the stress group.

2044.prule: Primary stress is lexically specified ('unpredictable') and falls on one of the last three syllables of the stress group (base + affixes + monosyllabic clitics); stress on an open syllable is realised as length, and under affixation stress keeps its position relative to the final syllable. No weight or fixed-position rule is stated.
2044.srule: Secondary stress is stated and 'predictable from primary stress': in a reduplicated word it falls on the syllable that carries stress in the base; otherwise on the second syllable after the primary stress or on the third syllable before it; it is deleted when that third-preceding syllable is itself preceded by a stressed syllable (apparent second-preceding cases are due to vowel deletion). Same correlates as primary stress (incl. length on an open syllable) but weaker, especially in pitch.
2044.quote: The nucleus of each stress group is a syllable marked by increased intensity which also causes slight rising of pitch and a tendency towards length. ... The base of the stress group is normally made up of two syllables. Upon this base is built the stress group by addition of various grammatical units. ... A single syllable pronoun, although included in the rhythmic unity of the stress group, does not affect the placement of stress. ... The occurrence of stress in any word is unpredictable but it defines a syllable on which it falls as being one of the three last syllables of the stress group.…

2049.heavy: A final syllable containing a diphthong ('palavras terminadas em ditongo'; Crowell 1979: 'when the final syllable contains a diphthong'). Nonato analyses diphthongs as underlying vowel sequences (accent goes to the penultimate vowel, then glide formation), and declines a Latin-type weight rule on analytic grounds; the surface facts are the same under either analysis. Bororo syllables are open ('a estrutura silábica do bororo não admite seqüências de consoantes', p. 19), so closed-syllable weight does not arise; only VV counts.
2049.prule: Surface: stress on the penultimate syllable, except that a word whose final syllable contains a (falling) diphthong is stressed on the final syllable (kaˈnao̯ 'espinha', baˈɡai̯; Crowell 1979: penult loudest, 'when the final syllable contains a diphthong' the final is loudest). Source's own analysis: rule (17) assigns accent to the penultimate vowel of the word, then rule (18) glide-formation merges adjacent non-low vowels into one syllable, applying cyclically; stressed monosyllables are underlyingly /VV/ and surface long (/baa/ -> ˈbaː 'aldeia'). Nonato explicitly considers and rejects a Latin-type weight rule.

2050.dq: In Ku Waru, all polysyllabic words when pronounced carefully in isolation have within them a single syllable with a pitch peak which is higher than that of any other syllable within the word; for about 80% of them it is the final syllable.
2050.dloc: Section 3 'Aspects of Ku Waru segmental phonology and prosody', pp. 43-44 (extract pp. 5-6; page headed '...ordinary means 43' below Table 1, running onto '44 Alan Rumsey'); fn. 8 p. 43 (monosyllables, naá vs na); p. 46 (extract p. 8) for 'nor is any role played by a distinction of that kind among syllables within words... the Ku Waru tone system' Same statement in Rumsey 2007, Anthropological Linguistics 49: 237-238, fn. 4-5 pp. 272-273.
2050.prule: Culminative lexical high pitch, not stress: every word has exactly one syllable with a pitch peak; by default (about 80% of polysyllabic words) it is the word-final syllable, and non-final peaks are lexically or grammatically specified (koma 'carry on one's shoulder' vs kóma 'wet'; toba hit:FUT.3s vs tóba hit:NF.3s). The peak syllable is explicitly not longer or louder; final syllables are the shortest and a final high vowel may drop in connected speech. Author's label: 'pitch-accent' (Merlan & Rumsey 1991:324), 'tone system' (Rumsey 2007 fn. 4, following Hyman 2006; Rumsey 2010: 46).
2050.srule: None: each word has 'a single syllable with a pitch peak' and 'nor is any role played by a distinction of that kind [strong vs weak] among syllables within words' (Rumsey 2010: 43, 46); the prominence is pitch, not stress, and no secondary prominence is described.

2051.tone: Source (sec. 2.4, p. 8) sets up a phonemic H/L register contrast on the syllable (template (C1)(C2)V(C3)/T, p. 6) with a rising contour tone, and states in the same paragraph that stress and phonation type are not distinctive. Polysyllables carry one of two melodies determined by the first syllable (H-L-L or L-H-L, p. 9), i.e. a single H peak within the first two syllables -- this could be re-analysed as a pitch-accent/word-tone system, but the author frames it as tone and never locates phonetic prominence. Summary point 4 (p. 15) repeats that the rising tone on checked syllables is not phonologically distinctive. Takeuchi 2014 (Kobe Gaidai Ronso 64(3), fn. 5 p. 60, in the copy consulted) follows Nishida in marking two tones, H and L, and says nothing about stress.

2055.dq: Una palabra, en función del número de sus sílabas, podrá presentar alguna de las combinaciones anteriores. Cuando una palabra es empleada en un contexto sintáctico, la posición que ocupa puede repercutir en la posterior e irremediable modificación tonal (Bolekia 2008: 77); Levin's 5.1-5.3 examples are isolated citation-form words (nouns).

2055.prule: Two-level (H/L) lexical tone system; no positional word-stress rule is stated by any reachable modern source (only Clarke's 1848 missionary sketch says the accent is 'usually on the penultimate' in simple words, with a double accent in compounds and, in four-syllable words, 'usually on the first, as well as on the penultimate syllable'; see Tone). Bolekia (2008: 77; 2009: 11) describes prominence purely as high vs low tone (words mono- or bitonal, tone altered by syntactic position) and identifies phonological tone with what Spanish calls 'acento de intensidad'. Levin (1965, Batete dialect) marks an 'acento' whose position 'no es automático' and 'depende, sobre todo, de la estructura morfemática', with a secondary accent, while also recording a two-tone system (6.4).
2055.srule: Exists, placement not given: Levin states only 'Existe el acento secundario: /bubálè/ 'piedra' /matálè/ 'piedras'' (a grave-marked final syllable after the acute penult in two trisyllabic nouns); no rule for where secondary accent falls and nothing for other word lengths. Later descriptions (Bolekia 1991: 27-28; 2008: 77-78) give no secondary-stress rule either (Bolekia 1991 lists words 'con dos, tres o más acentos (en todas las posiciones)' without ranking them).

2055.tone: All reachable modern sources call Bubi a two-tone (H/L) language: Levin 1965 6.4 ('dos tonos diferentes: /poto/ 'deidad' /potó/ 'gracias''), Bolekia 2008: 77 ('dos tonos puntuales, como la lengua bubi'; words mono-/bitonal; H-L, L-H, H-H sequences; tone modified by syntactic position), Bolekia 2009: 11 (high tone written with acute/grave, low unmarked; the high-tone vowel is likened to the stressed vowel of Spanish casa [kása]). Bolekia gives no stress-placement rule and equates phonological tone with Castilian intensity accent. Older missionary impressions: Clarke 1848: 10-11 'In simple words the accent is usually on the penultimate; but in compound words, and in words with the double catching sound, there is a double accent... In words of four syllables the accent is usually on the first, as well as on the penultimate syllable'; Juanola 1890: 13, item 12: 'Agudas, graves y esdrújulas; v. gr.: Mutó, grande; lama, todos; ñéola, abuela.' tn.quote: Par contre les variations de hauteur mélodique ont une fonction distinctive. ... nous ne retenons que les deux extrêmes comme phonologiques: il y a une opposition entre le ton haut et le ton non-haut. ... Pour le moment nous sommes donc amenés à poser deux unités distinctives de hauteur mélodique ou tonèmes: - un tonème haut /H/ se réalisant moyen en syllabe finale non accentuée et haut ailleurs, - un tonème bas /B/ se réalisant moyen en syllabe accentuée, bas descendant en finale absolue et bas ailleurs. tn.translation: By contrast, variations of pitch have a distinctive function. ... we retain only the two extremes as phonological: there is an opposition between high tone and non-high tone. ... For the moment we are therefore led to posit two distinctive units of pitch, or tonemes: - a high toneme /H/ realised mid in a final unaccented syllable and high elsewhere, - a low toneme /B/ realised mid in an accented syllable, low-falling in absolute final position and low elsewhere. These tonemes have the syllable as their domain.

2058.prule: Dynamic (expiratory) stress, 'in most cases fixed on a definite syllable'. Bare stems (word = stem): second syllable (adá, didé, xiláb, q'apú, džidár, sermísaǧ - the trisyllable also takes σ2). Inflected and derived words: position set by the grammatical form / affix - general present and future initial (čáǧari, q'éč'ira), debitive second (čaǧári), -lu adjective final (džurǧamlú); stress alone distinguishes present from debitive (čáǧari vs čaǧári, írqiri vs irqíri). tn.translation: Like all zone C languages, the ebujá of Yambuli has two basic tones: low and high. These two tones, already seen in the examples cited so far, are written respectively by the absence of any mark and by the acute accent. Beside the simple tones there are however also the complex rising and falling tones. The falling tone is written with the circumflex and the rising tone with the inverted circumflex. ... Tones are instable in Bugan, a part of the lexicon can be pronounced with either of two tones ... (p. 141) ... 2.1.2.2. Derived words. 2065.prule: None stated. The only prosodic statement in the sole description is that no suprasegmental phonemes were found ('fonem suprasegmental atau prosodi jelas tidak ada'), i.e. stress, length and tone are not contrastive. The source gives no position for (non-contrastive) word stress, marks no stress in any transcription, and describes no phrase-level prominence. Translation of the quote: 'As we set out above, we found only segmental phonemes, that is, consonants and vowels only, whereas anything involving suprasegmental phonemes or prosody is clearly absent.'

2065.tone: The source denies suprasegmental phonemes, so no tone is reported. 'Tekanan' there means emphasis/clarity; no syllable position is named, so it is not a stress rule.

It comprises the following languages: Zùl, Barang, Dììr, Bili, Nyámzax, Lundur, Pos. From 1995 to 2004, I have done fieldwork on: Dììr, Bili (Buli), Nyámzax (Langas), Pos (Polci) and Luri. 2066.idn: Bili (Buli); no narrower variety named (the ISO [uly] form distinguishes Babban Buli and Mulan varieties; Caron does not say which his data represent); data: author's fieldwork 1995-2004 on Diir, Bili (Buli), Nyamzax, Pos and Luri…
2066.tone: Two tone levels (Lo = à, Hi = a) for Buli, by the author's classification of the non-Polci-proper Polci-cluster lects ('the others'), with Bili explicitly enumerated in the cluster; Polci proper (Po) and Zaar (Za) have three levels. No statement about stress or accent for any South-Bauchi West lect; the word 'accent' in Caron 2003 (p. 2) and 2006 (fn. 3) means only the acute/grave tone diacritics ('Hi is marked with an acute accent; Lo with a grave'). Corroboration at second hand: Caron's 2002 review reports that Cosper 1999 marks two tones for all eight Barawa lects including Buli.

2067.dq: Stress is penultimate, and non-phonemic in all non-ambivalent instances. High vocoids [i] and [u] are accordingly analysed as vowels in all occurrences, thus simplifying stress specification as predictably penultimate.
2067.dloc: p. 62, section 1 'Synchronic phonology', first paragraph; language list p. 60; acknowledgement of the Bulu assistant in note 3, p. 91.
2067.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable; it is non-phonemic (predictable). Syllables are (C)V and the high vocoids i and u always count as syllabic vowels, so the penult is counted over vowels with no glide/diphthong parsing. The statement covers all seven Kimbe languages (Bali, Vitu, Bulu, Bola, Harua, Meramera, Nakanai) at once; Bulu is one of them and the author elicited its word lists and texts himself.
2067.srule: Not mentioned in Johnston 1982 (sec. 1 'Synchronic phonology', pp. 62-64 read in full): the only stress statement is the family-wide 'Stress is penultimate, and non-phonemic... predictably penultimate'; nothing on secondary or rhythmic stress for Bulu or any Kimbe language.
2067.quote: The syllable pattern in all of the Kimbe languages id [sic] (C)V. Stress is penultimate, and non-phonemic in all non-ambivalent instances. High vocoids [i] and [u] are accordingly analysed as vowels in all occurrences, thus simplifying stress specification as predictably penultimate.
